summary: Raises questions about the ARPANET topology shown in RFC 597, in particular how well connected some nodes are. RFC 613 replies to it.

plainLanguage.summary: Someone looked at the map of the network and asked whether the way the computers were linked was a good idea.

subtitle: A short list of questions about how well connected the ARPANET map of November 1973 was.

tldr.problem: RFC 597 showed the November 1973 ARPANET topology, and the author wondered whether some nodes were too heavily connected while some regions were too weakly connected.
tldr.mechanism: The author asks two questions: whether IMPs should have no more than three connections, and whether the Boston, San Francisco and Los Angeles areas should be pulled into loops like the Washington area.
tldr.outcome: It poses questions and sets no rules. The metadata lists it as updating RFC 597 and as updated by RFC 613, whose summary says it responds to these points.

today: The document metadata lists RFC 603 as updating RFC 597 and as updated by RFC 613. Its status is recorded as Unknown, and it is a historical discussion of the 1973 network map.

sections.title: The Map Under Review
sections.content:
RFC 603 is a response to RFC 597, which was about host status. J. D. Burchfiel of BBN-TENEX dated it 31 December, 1973 and says he has several questions about the November 1973 ARPANET topographical map.

The document is one page long and consists of two numbered questions. It proposes no protocol and sets no requirements.
sections.plainLanguage: Someone studied a map of the network and wrote down two questions about it.

sections.title: Too Many Links on One Node
sections.content: The first question is about AMES, which is 4-connected: four network connections will go down if its IMP fails. The author asks whether there is some aspiration that IMPs should be no more than three connected.
sections.plainLanguage: If one switch has four wires plugged into it, all four stop working when it breaks. The author asks if four is too many.

sections.title: Loops Around Regions
sections.content:
The second question concerns the seven IMPs in the Washington area, which are arranged into a loop. That guarantees local communication can continue if one connection fails, and the author thinks it is probably a worthwhile preparation for area routing.

He contrasts this with Boston: a break between MIT-IPC and MIT-MAC would force them to communicate through a 12-hop path through Washington. He suggests a short, inexpensive connection between Harvard and Lincoln Labs as a remedy, and asks whether there is a plan to pull the Boston, San Francisco and Los Angeles areas into loops like Washington's.
sections.plainLanguage: A ring of friends can still pass notes if one link breaks. Some neighbourhoods had no ring, so a broken link meant a very long detour.
